data.title: mzio launches first vendor-neutral AI control layer for multimodal mass spectrometry data processing
data.description:
BREMEN, Germany —

mzio GmbH announces the launch of mzassist, a vendor-neutral AI and automation control layer for multimodal mass spectrometry data processing on its trusted, open-source mzmine platform.

mzassist uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) open standard introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, now supported by many AI agents and platforms, to connect mzio’s established, vendor-agnostic mzmine platform to a user’s approved MCP-compatible AI assistant. For the lab user, this simplifies set up and implementation of complete mass spectrometry data processing workflows in natural language; importing raw data, selecting templates, configuring parameters, running batches and summarizing results to increase operational consistency and free up lab time to focus on scientific input. 

mzio shared exclusive preview access to mzassist with the scientific community in a workshop at the 8th Munich Metabolomics Meeting on October 13th, 2026, ahead of public release, giving researchers hands-on experience with the technology in LC-MS, GC-MS and MALDI-MS and gaining valuable feedback. 

The mzassist approach draws a clear line on security and scientific control in the laboratory: the raw mass spec data stays on the lab’s own computer, and users control the information that is shared with the AI via opt-in / opt-out protocols. Because the AI tool is only active when enabled by the user, the user decides at every stage how much to hand over, either delegating the entire workflow or enabling manual intervention at any stage. Parameter decisions are made by deterministic mzmine algorithms rather than the language model, and labs connect the AI assistant that their IT and data protection teams have already approved, increasing accessibility and speed for mass spectrometry data management. 

“The AI story in lab informatics has now moved from ‘can we use it?’ to ‘how do we use it responsibly?’” Dr. Ansgar Korf, CEO and co-founder of mzio comments. “mzassist brings together two key factors in mass spectrometry data management: the reliability of our long established, trusted mzmine system to handle the scientific decisions, and new accessibility through AI. The lab chooses which AI assistant to trust, and mzmine stays the authoritative environment for the data analysis itself. That combination makes AI practical in a mass spec workflow without compromising reproducibility or the vendor-neutral position that mzmine has held since 2005.”

mzassist can also help lab users get started faster with both existing and new analytical methods, explaining processing steps, algorithms and parameters, and supporting spectral library building. The parameter estimator analyzes a selection of the user’s raw data files and derives suitable processing parameters, and the auto optimizer then benchmarks and identifies the settings that perform best on the actual data. 

“Parameter estimation and optimization in mzassist are data-driven algorithms, not guesswork by a language model,” adds Dr. Steffen Heuckeroth, CTO and co-founder of mzio. “The estimator derives parameters directly from the signals in a lab’s raw data, with consistent results every time. Users and AI agents can both call on these tools to get the same measurable basis for deciding which parameters to use, and every analysis started through mzassist is documented as a complete mzmine workflow file that records each processing step and parameter, meaning AI assistance increases productivity while keeping results reproducible and traceable." 

mzassist will be available with mzmine 4.11 October 2026. Laboratories can connect the AI tool that fits their own IT, data protection and compliance requirements. It is included in mzmine COMMUNITY for academic users and in mzmine PRO for commercial customers, supporting mzio’s mission to empower researchers and analysts around the world with reliable tools for mass spectrometry data analysis. More information is available at mzio.io.

data.title: Flagship blends three biotech startups to form Etcelera
data.description:
The biotechnology startup creator Flagship Pioneering is rolling three of its fledgling companies into a new venture called Etcelera, which is combining artificial intelligence with an array of drug discovery tools to try to predict which experimental medicines might succeed in the clinic.

Flagship announced Thursday that the new startup has been formed from the parts of three former portfolio companies: Etiome, Cellarity and Empress Therapeutics. It’s led by Adrian “Ad” Rawcliffe, the former CEO of Adaptimmune and a veteran of GSK.

“Each had a piece of this puzzle, and if you bring them together, then we have the opportunity to go beyond what each of them was doing and redefine cause-and-effect in biology,” Rawcliffe said in an interview.

Etcelera claims that combining the technologies of these three companies with Flagship’s in-house AI capabilities should help its scientists pinpoint novel disease drivers and uncover small molecule medicines to target them. It also believes these drugs will have better odds than those discovered with traditional approaches. Rawcliffe said the datasets and technology developed by its three forebears could be useful in gauging which drugs might fail in human testing.

“If you feed appropriate machine learning enough biological language, then maybe it can infer what biology looks like, where meaning lies in biology and can predict what will happen in biological systems,” Rawcliffe said.

Biotech companies have long spoken enthusiastically about the ability of high-powered computing tools to upend drug discovery and cure many diseases. The hype has sparked blowback that companies using AI to design medicines may be overstating their potential and underestimating the complexities of human biology. Multiple biotechs built on AI technology have struggled in the public markets. 

Yet private investment in AI drug discovery companies has accelerated in 2026. Several have raised large funding rounds, and one company, Iambic Therapeutics, recently went public. (AI giant Anthropic, which has invested heavily in life sciences research, could soon follow.) 

Etcelera is combining AI tools with a series of other strategies. And one edge Rawcliffe believes the company has is its use of “perturbation data,” a way of seeing how a cell would respond to disruption, such as by silencing a gene or introducing a chemical.

The company intends to develop medicines for hematological conditions, immune diseases and metabolic-fibrotic disorders. It’s starting out with a handful of programs for conditions such as myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia.

“Our vision is to build a compounding AI system that becomes a definitive source of novel medicines that are more likely to succeed in clinical development than any prior technology,” said Alec Reynolds, a senior partner at Flagship and chair of Etcelera’s board, in a statement.

Flagship will shuttle an oral sickle cell disease drug that Cellarity discovered into a different, standalone company, the firm said.

No new funding was announced alongside Etcelera’s public launch. The three biotechs it’s built on had banked $374 million in venture capital backing prior to the merger, which Rawcliffe said will help carry the company further.

The new biotech will retain a 2022 partnership between Novo and Cellarity formed to find a small molecule treatment for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis. A second alliance with an unnamed large pharmaceutical firm is also in the works, Rawcliffe said.

“We’ll be looking for partners who bring substantial disease or therapy area expertise to pair with this platform,” he said.

Etcelera’s name is a kind of portmanteau of “et cetera” and “accelerate,” an idea Rawcliffe said was born out of the theory that simulating early drug development on a computer could speed up the iterative process of finding new drugs.

data.title: The molecule was fine. The moment wasn’t.
data.description:
The pharmaceutical industry is very good at looking forward. We spend enormous amounts of time, capital, and talent searching for what comes next: the next molecule, the next mechanism, the next breakthrough. We should. Discovery is one of the engines of medical progress. But I believe there is another source of innovation—and value—that our industry sometimes overlooks.

Markets and science change. Treatment paradigms change. Patient expectations change. Technologies improve. Commercial models evolve.

And when the world around a medicine changes, the strategic value of that medicine can change with it. Obesity may be one of the clearest examples.

A market transformed

In September 2014, the FDA approved an oral combination therapy for chronic weight management. By mid-2015, it had become the most-prescribed branded anti-obesity medication in the United States. Three years later, its manufacturer filed for Chapter 11.

It would be easy to read that history as a verdict on the medicine. I think that misses a more complicated story.

The obesity treatment environment of a decade ago looked very different from the one we see today. Coverage was limited. Obesity was still fighting for recognition as a chronic disease requiring medical treatment. Patient awareness was lower. Physician engagement was different. And the commercial infrastructure surrounding medical weight management was far less developed.

Then GLP-1s changed the category.

Their pharmacology represented an extraordinary advance. But their impact extended well beyond the medicines themselves. That’s because they helped change the conversation around obesity.

Treatment became increasingly normalized and patient awareness grew dramatically. Physicians became more engaged. Payers and employers were forced to confront questions about access and coverage. And millions of people gained direct experience with pharmacological weight management. The market didn't simply grow. The context changed. And that distinction matters.

When the market changes, look again

Pharmaceutical companies spend enormous amounts of time searching for new assets. I believe there is another source of potential value hiding in plain sight: established medicines whose potential may have been defined by yesterday's market rather than today's. That doesn't mean every commercially unsuccessful medicine deserves another chance. Far from it.

The discipline is understanding why an asset underperformed.

Was there a problem with the medicine itself? Was the patient population poorly understood? Was the commercial model wrong? Was access too limited? Did the treatment paradigm evolve? Or did the medicine simply arrive before the market around it was ready?

Those are very different problems.

Distinguishing between them requires more than optimism. It requires rigorous analysis of the medicine, the market, the patient need, the competitive environment, and—importantly—the capabilities required to create value under a different set of conditions.

Sometimes the medicine hasn't changed. Everything around it has.

That 2014 medicine is naltrexone HCl/bupropion HCl.

In June of this year, Azurity Pharmaceuticals acquired naltrexone HCl/bupropion HCl along with a related portfolio.

Our decision wasn't based on nostalgia for an overlooked asset. It reflected a disciplined view of how the market surrounding that asset has changed—and how we believe our capabilities can create value within that changed environment.

The obesity category today is fundamentally different from the category naltrexone HCl/bupropion HCl entered more than a decade ago. Patient awareness has grown exponentially. Physician engagement has increased. Treatment has become more normalized. The commercial infrastructure has evolved. And millions more patients now have experience with pharmacological approaches to chronic weight management.

We also don't believe there is a single answer to obesity. The extraordinary growth of the category has reinforced how diverse patients' needs, experiences, and treatment journeys can be.

When the conditions surrounding an established medicine change, its strategic value can change with them. Recognizing those inflection points is an important part of the model we are building at Azurity.

The model matters

We look for established medicines and therapeutic categories where we believe there is unrealized value—and where our development, regulatory, commercial, market access, and global capabilities can make a difference.

That value can emerge in different ways: through formulation or delivery innovation, by better serving patient populations whose needs remain unmet, by expanding access, by applying a different commercialization model, or by pursuing more thoughtful lifecycle development.

And sometimes, as with naltrexone HCl/bupropion HCl, the market surrounding an established medicine has fundamentally changed.

The common denominator isn't the product. It’s the model.

We've built Azurity to pursue multiple opportunities like these simultaneously. Our diversified, multi-franchise model allows us to identify opportunities that might not fit the traditional pharmaceutical playbook and apply the capabilities needed to develop, commercialize, and scale them.

That is important because identifying an overlooked asset is only the beginning. Value is created through what happens next: disciplined capital allocation, development and regulatory execution, market access, commercialization, lifecycle management, and increasingly, the ability to deploy technology and data across all of them.

This isn't about collecting old medicines. It's about building a repeatable capability for recognizing value that others may not see—and having the operating model to act on it.

Innovation beyond discovery

None of this diminishes the importance of discovering new medicines. We need breakthrough science, novel mechanisms, and new therapies. But innovation doesn't end with discovery.

Innovation can often be found in reformulating an established medicine or finding a better way to deliver it. It can mean reaching a population whose needs haven't been adequately served. Sometimes it relates to applying a different commercial or access model. And sometimes it’s defined by looking again when the world around a medicine has changed.

That is where patient need and business opportunity can intersect.

Medicines are necessarily evaluated in controlled clinical settings, but patients don't live in clinical trials. They live in the complexity of the real world—with jobs, families, budgets, routines, preferences, and needs that evolve over years. Understanding that reality can reveal opportunities that aren't always obvious when we look at medicine solely through the lens of novelty.

Look again

The lesson from naltrexone HCl/bupropion HCl isn't that every medicine deserves another chance. Most won't.

The lesson is that markets change—and disciplined companies should be willing to revisit assumptions when they do.

At Azurity, that is an increasingly important part of how we think about growth. We look for opportunities where patient need, market evolution, and our capabilities intersect—and where we believe we can create value that others may not see.

Naltrexone HCl/bupropion HCl is one example. Across our industry, there is a vast landscape of established medicines, overlooked assets, underserved patient populations, and evolving therapeutic categories. Markets will continue to change. Patient needs will continue to evolve. And medicines whose potential may not have been fully realized under one set of circumstances may look very different under another.

For companies built to recognize those changes—and with the capabilities to act on them—there exists a remarkably broad landscape for continued growth.

Innovation isn't only about seeing what comes next. Sometimes it's about looking differently at what is already there.

data.title: ESMO ‘26: A cancer vaccine debate, Roche’s KRAS progress and Amgen’s ‘unprecedented’ data
data.description:
Today, BioPharma Dive is highlighting some important clinical trial updates presented at the annual European Society for Medical Oncology meeting. Over the last few days, several large pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies released detailed study data on new and emerging medicines for an array of different tumors.

Below are three notable storylines and a look at how they’re being interpreted by investors and analysts.

A cancer vaccine debate

The Phase 3 success of Moderna and Merck & Co.’s vaccine intismeran autogene in melanoma was a “genuine scientific milestone” in melanoma treatment, wrote RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh. The 42% reduction in the relative risk of recurrence or death associated with treatment in that study, which was presented in detail at ESMO over the weekend, is a “clinically meaningful and likely approvable result,” he added in a note on Saturday.

Wall Street investors have had a different interpretation. Since the results were released prematurely on Thursday afternoon, Moderna’s share price — which had skyrocketed over the last few months — has plunged by double digits. Multiple industry analysts have defended Moderna since then, calling the reaction a “sell-the-news” response to data that had met expectations. Yet that optimism was countered by worries that Moderna’s current valuation is only justified if intismeran works in other tumor types. Investors are also skeptical about the manufacturing and commercial potential of a patient-specific therapy like intismeran.

Melanoma is known to be particularly susceptible to immune-boosting treatments because of the number of mutations these tumors express. Those characteristics made melanoma the ideal setting for a first-of-its-kind therapy such as intismeran. But the results don’t guarantee success elsewhere, and investigators interviewed by BioPharma Dive declined to make any predictions ahead of key readouts in lung, kidney or bladder tumors.

As an “individualized neoantigen therapy,” intismeran is produced through a complicated process that involves sequencing patient tumors and using that information to create a specialized vaccine. In the Phase 3 trial, for instance, patients waited a median of 64 days before receiving their first dose. The treatment turnaround was less critical in the post-surgical “adjuvant” setting, where intismeran’s objective was to keep disease from returning. But Moderna and Merck also hope the therapy can be an option in cancers that are actively spreading.

One study investigator is hopeful. For intismeran to be a practical solution, Moderna and Merck will need to help oncologists prepare for use early on, said Janice Mehnert, director of melanoma and cutaneous medical oncology at NYU Langone Health.

“I do think that’s something that’s manageable,” Mehnert said. “As technology gets better and workflows change, we’ll get better.” — Jonathan Gardner

Roche’s KRAS progress

Roche is a relative latecomer in the push to develop medicines for cancers driven by tough-to-drug “KRAS” mutations. But it has a chance to leapfrog some competitors thanks to the progress of a drug called divarasib. 

In July, Roche disclosed that divarasib topped two marketed medicines — Bristol Myers Squibb’s Krazati and Amgen’s Lumakras — in a Phase 3 trial. That study tested all three drugs in patients whose non-small cell lung tumors have a particular KRAS mutation known as “G12C.” Roche didn’t provide specifics at the time, but said that in people with these alterations, divarasib was associated with statistical improvements on measures of survival as well as tumor progression. 

Detailed data at ESMO suggest divarasib has now “set a new bar” in this setting, wrote Stifel analyst Laura Prendergast. Divarasib cut the risk of death or disease progression by 42% and lowered the likelihood of death, specifically, by 44%. A primary analysis found that participants on Roche’s medicine lived a median of roughly 18 months, versus a year for people on Krazati or Lumakras.

Importantly, the results “confirm” a survival benefit for divarasib that first-generation drugs weren’t able to achieve, wrote RBC analyst Huynh. And even though patients on divarasib were treated nearly twice as long, it was still associated with lower rates of severe adverse events or treatment-related side effects that were deemed “Grade 3” or worse. 

During an ESMO presentation, one researcher described the findings as an “immense innovation.” But he also cautioned that both Krazati and Lumakras have run into trouble with insurers and that divarasib might struggle, too, as it wasn’t tested against the standard chemotherapy docetaxel, Huynh wrote. 

Roche is optimistic. On an earnings call last week, executives cited the study data in upgrading their peak sales expectations for divarasib from 2 billion Swiss francs to 3 billion, equivalent to about $3.6 billion annually. Krazati and Lumakras respectively banked $205 million and $363 million last year. — Ben Fidler

Amgen’s ‘unprecedented’ lung cancer data

“Small cell” lung cancer accounts for around 10% to 15% of lung tumors and is known as the tougher of the two major forms of the disease to treat. Typically linked to smoking, these tumors grow and spread more quickly than “non-small cell” lung cancers. Many people already have “extensive stage” disease by the time they’re diagnosed, too, meaning their cancers have already spread to both lungs or other organs. 

Since its approval in 2024, Amgen’s Imdelltra has established itself as a go-to treatment for patients whose disease has progressed following chemotherapy. That use has made Imdelltra one of the big biotech’s fastest-growing products. Sales reached $627 million in 2025 and are on track to surpass $1 billion this year. 

Data presented at ESMO and simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine could drive those figures substantially higher. In September, Amgen revealed, without details, that a combination of Imdelltra and the cancer immunotherapy Imfinzi topped Imfinzi alone when given as a “maintenance” therapy following initial treatment. Over the weekend, Amgen revealed that combination reduced the risk of death by 58% versus Imfinzi alone. Those on the former regimen lived a median of 21.1 months, compared to 12.7 months for Imfinzi recipients. 

Those findings were met with a “standing ovation” at ESMO and described by an independent researcher as “fundamentally chang[ing] the outcome” of ES-SCLC treatment, wrote TD Cowen analyst Yaron Werber. Importantly, the drug combination’s safety was “manageable” and “comparable” to what’s seen with Imfinzi alone, he added.  

For Amgen, the study “validates earlier-line use” of Imdelltra, which the company is focused on moving into initial treatment, wrote Mizuho Securities analyst Salim Syed. Consensus estimates already have the drug peaking at $4 billion in annual sales. But approvals in additional treatment lines could open up a $9.6 billion market opportunity, Werber wrote. 

The “unprecedented” survival benefit “sets a clear new standard of care,” wrote William Blair analyst Matt Phipps, in a separate note. — Ben Fidler

data.title: Appian and PSI CRO Form Strategic Partnership to Advance AI-driven Clinical Trial Operations
data.description:
ZUG, Switzerland —

28 October 2026 – Appian [Nasdaq: APPN] and PSI CRO announced today the launch of their first joint AI-powered process orchestration solution. The new offering automates clinical trial site identification and selection across therapeutic areas, indications, and geographies.

The live solution is the first step in a shared vision by PSI and Appian to build a scalable platform that connects automation, AI-powered capabilities, and process orchestration across the full clinical trial lifecycle. Together, the companies are creating a foundation designed to improve efficiency, transparency, and speed across complex clinical trial processes.

AI and process orchestration for complex site selection 

Clinical trial site selection is a highly coordinated process involving multiple stakeholders, large volumes of documentation, and parallel activities across countries and regions. The new solution brings previously manual, decentralized steps into a single digital process, from project initiation through the subsequent stages of site selection.

Recognized by Gartner as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies (BOAT), we believe the Appian Platform provides the foundation for this solution. It identifies and selects the most suitable study sites for sponsors, providing greater end-to-end visibility and enabling faster execution across the site selection process.

The solution goes beyond task automation to orchestrate the end-to-end process, connecting people, data, systems, and AI in a single workflow. It coordinates activities across teams and geographies and automates information and document processing. It also manages routing and exceptions, providing real-time insight into process performance. 

The solution integrates with PSI’s core systems and data warehouse, as well as Appian’s AI and process intelligence capabilities. The integrated solution creates a scalable foundation for faster decisions, greater consistency, and continuous improvement.

Starting point for a long-term platform strategy

The site selection solution puts PSI’s platform vision into practice. It combines PSI’s focus on predictable clinical trial delivery with Appian’s process automation and AI capabilities.

“The AI-powered clinical trial site selection solution is an important step in how we are rethinking and connecting our operational processes,” says Kirill Soldatov, Head of Process Improvement at PSI. “PSI is known for our ability to deliver complex clinical trials on time. Building a more connected operational model through automation, AI-powered capabilities, and process orchestration within our existing workflows creates a scalable foundation for more predictable, accurate, and timely site selection worldwide, with the goal to further reduce or eliminate non-enrolling sites and patient enrollment delays.”

“This initial project demonstrates the value AI can create when it is embedded in business processes. The solution helps PSI process information faster with automation and manage processes with greater transparency with orchestration. Through our strategic partnership with PSI, we aim to create a flexible, long-term foundation for further automation and innovation,” adds Alexander Motie, Regional Vice President DACH & Eastern Europe at Appian.

With the first solution now live, PSI and Appian will build on this foundation by evaluating further use cases to extend AI-powered process orchestration across the clinical trial lifecycle. The goal is to shorten clinical studies and increase predictability, thus introducing new products to market and driving down costs for consumers. 

Find out how life sciences companies can use AI automation for faster speed to market here.

data.title: Lilly shuffles business structure; Novartis writes off part of Avidity deal
data.description:
Today, a brief rundown of news involving Eli Lilly and Novartis, as well as updates from Astellas Pharma, Pfizer and Bolt Biotherapeutics that you may have missed.

Patrik Jonsson will retire from Eli Lilly at the end of 2026, completing a 36-year run at the Indianapolis-based drugmaker. Jonsson started at Lilly as a sales representative in Sweden in 1990 and rose through the ranks to eventually lead the company’s global pharmaceutical business, “Lilly International.” Once he steps down, Lilly’s U.S. and international divisions will combine into an entity called “Lilly Global Markets” and be headed by Ilya Yuffa, a Lilly executive vice president and head of global customer capabilities. The new structure will “accelerate decision-making, increase scalability” and help broaden access to medicines globally, Lilly said. — Ben Fidler

Novartis will take a $1.9 billion impairment charge after seeing an experimental drug it acquired in a $12 billion buyout of Avidity Biosciences fail a late-stage trial in August. The Swiss drugmaker revealed the write-off in its latest quarterly earnings report Tuesday, which included sales figures that topped Wall Street’s expectations and news that the company hiked its 2026 financial forecasts. Novartis is facing multiple key patent expirations in the near future and is looking to key drugs in its late-stage pipeline, like Avidity’s del-desiran, to spur future growth. Though that drug fell short in a study in a rare muscle-wasting disease, the company hasn’t given up on its approval chances. An open-label extension to that trial is ongoing, and executives told analysts Tuesday that they assume Novartis will need to run an additional Phase 3 study. — Delilah Alvarado

Astellas Pharma has secured from Australian biotech Audax Biosciences an option to license an experimental cancer immunotherapy nearing human testing. Called DAX-044, the therapy is an “antibody-cytokine fusion” designed to deliver the immune protein IL-12 into cancer cells. In a statement, Astellas said DAX-044 has “best-in-class” potential. The deal involves $285 million in up front and future option payments, and could include another $1.05 billion in additional consideration if certain milestones are met. Phase 1 testing should begin in 2027, Astellas said. — Ben Fidler

The Food and Drug Administration has expanded use of a two-drug regimen involving Pfizer’s cancer medicine Talzenna and the hormone therapy Xtandi. The combination was first approved in 2023 for certain patients with metastatic prostate cancer who’d stopped responding to hormone treatments. The new clearance makes treatment available earlier, when the benefits might be greater. The approval was based on study results showing the regimen cut the risk of cancer progression or death by more than half when compared to Xtandi and a placebo. — Delilah Alvarado

Prana Therapeutics is going public through a reverse merger with Bolt Biotherapeutics. The stock-for-stock deal announced Friday came alongside a $120 million private financing that’ll help fund the company through 2027 and into the following year. Prana is developing multi-pronged antibody drugs designed to last longer and require infrequent dosing. Its lead asset, PRA-216, zeroes in on the proteins TSLP and IL-4Rα and is in mid-stage testing for atopic dermatitis, asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. A second prospect is also being developed for atopic dermatitis but aims at a different target, IL-31. Data from first-in-human studies are expected next year. — Delilah Alvarado

data.title: Court rejects Novo bid to block Lilly obesity drug ads
data.description:
Dive Brief:

  • A federal judge denied Novo’s request to block an Eli Lilly advertising campaign comparing the companies’ respective obesity medicines Wegovy and Zepbound.  
  • Novo argued the advertisements used outdated studies to compare higher doses of Lilly’s medicines to lower doses of Novo’s products. The campaign caused “irreparable harm” and didn’t account for a more recently approved, higher-dose form of Wegovy, the company claimed in court documents.   
  • U.S. District Judge Zahid Quraishi ruled Monday that Novo failed to prove its case, as Wegovy prescription volume didn’t fall when the commercials aired and those ads acknowledged the existence of the higher-dose product. In an email to BioPharma Dive, a Novo spokesperson said the ruling didn’t “decide the question of whether Lilly’s advertising is false and misleading.”

Dive Insight:

Novo and Lilly are engaged in one of the most intense commercial battles in pharmaceutical history. Both are vying for control of a market opportunity Wall Street analysts expect to exceed $100 billion by 2030.

Novo had an early lead on its top rival. But since then, Lilly has grabbed the momentum. Zepbound bested the original Wegovy in a head-to-head trial, and Lilly quickly followed the launch of Novo’s Wegovy pill with an oral alternative of its own.

Along the way, tirzepatide, which Lilly sells as Zepbound for obesity and Mounjaro for diabetes, has become the industry’s best-selling product. The drugmaker’s outsized revenue numbers and healthy pipeline of follow-on prospects have propelled shares ever higher, helping it become biopharma’s first-ever trillion-dollar company — all while Novo’s value has sputtered.

Novo sued Lilly in July, claiming the emphasis of the head-to-head trial in Lilly’s promotions constituted deceptive advertising. The ruling handed down Monday was on Novo’s motion for a preliminary injunction to stop the campaign.

In a two-day hearing in August, the judge heard from Lilly U.S. finance chief Mark Stempel, who testified that Wegovy prescriptions remained stable during the April to July period the ads ran. Meanwhile, Novo witness Derrick Gastineau, the company’s U.S. vice president for obesity, “had not attempted to determine” any harm, Quraishi wrote in the ruling.

Furthermore, Quraishi wrote, Lilly altered the language in newer Zepbound ads following a cease-and-desist letter. Updated ads note the existence of high-dose Wegovy and specify that it wasn’t tested against Zepbound.

The judge also chastised Novo for advertising related to Ozempic, its GLP-1 shot for diabetes. Those ads claimed head-to-head superiority over a Lilly alternative called Trulicity, without revealing the availability of a higher-dose version, Quraishi wrote. 

The Novo spokesperson stated that the ruling “does not constitute a final resolution of the merits of Novo's false advertising claims and instead only addresses whether the court will issue such an order at this early stage of the proceedings.”

data.title: CRIO and Eli Lilly and Company win SCDM Innovation Award for Alzheimer's trial
data.description:
BOSTON —

CRIO, the leading provider of eSource technology for clinical research, received an SCDM Innovation Award with Eli Lilly and Company in the Clinical Data Science Implementation Excellence category at the SCDM 2026 Annual Conference. The awards program recognizes organizations that excel at integrating clinical data science through people, processes and technology. 

CRIO and Lilly were recognized for their collaboration on a global Phase 3 Alzheimer’s disease prevention trial spanning more than 120 sites in five countries and enrolling more than 2,000 patients. CRIO deployed its Central eSource platform for the pilot.

The traditional approach to source data collection would have required each of the trial's sites to independently translate a complex protocol into its own source templates, using a mix of paper documents, disconnected eSource systems and electronic health records. That model delays study startup and produces significant variability in how data is collected across sites. 

CRIO instead deployed a single, sponsor-driven electronic source template to participating sites at study activation. Sites could configure the template within Lilly-defined parameters, preserving site autonomy while ensuring consistency across the global study.

Key outcomes included: 

  • 70% site adoption: Sites across the global trial opted in voluntarily. 
  • 59% reduction in on-site monitoring visits: Central eSource enabled clinical research associates to monitor remotely, reducing travel requirements and associated costs. 
  • 30% lower cost per monitoring visit: The shift to remote monitoring lowered monitoring costs. 
  • 30-day faster site startup: Sites received protocol-driven source documents immediately upon activation. 
  • 24% improvement in monitoring effectiveness: Centralized data and real-time edit checks allowed monitors to review more patient visits per day. 

Lilly has already begun expanding Central eSource to additional studies beyond the original pilot. CRIO is building on lessons from this deployment in several ways: incorporating experienced sites into core template development to reduce site-level configuration work, advancing the EDC integration so future studies launch with it active from day one - eliminating SDV for integrated data points, reducing transcription errors, and expanding multilingual support to broaden the model's geographic reach.

“This pilot was one of the most ambitious central eSource deployments in the industry to date, and we’re honored to share this recognition with Lilly,” said Jonathan Andrus, co-CEO, CRIO. “Seventy percent of sites chose to opt in. That tells us the model works for the people doing the research, not just the sponsor, and it’s a strong signal that standardized source data is ready to transform clinical research on a global scale.” 

Andrus was also recognized with the Distinguished Service Award from SCDM. A member of the organization for nearly thirty years, he has served on the board for over 20 years, during which he has served as chair twice and currently serves as SCDM treasurer.

data.title: Another autoimmune CAR-T death; Treasury zeroes in on China deals
data.description:
Today, a brief rundown of news involving Bristol Myers Squibb and the U.S. Department of the Treasury, as well as updates from Gilead Sciences and Zymeworks that you may have missed.

A trial participant who received an experimental autoimmune cell therapy from Bristol Myers Squibb died 44 days later, the company said Friday. Following an infusion with “zola-cel” in a multiple sclerosis study, the trial participant experienced what Bristol Myers described as “late onset ... motor symptoms” that couldn’t be quelled by steroids and other drugs. The volunteer later developed septic pneumonia and died shortly afterward. Bristol Myers said no other deaths have been observed in that study or any other autoimmune disease trial of zola-cel. It also touted findings suggesting the therapy’s potential to “reset” the immune system in people with MS. Still, the company as well as Novartis previously paused multiple autoimmune cell therapy studies due to safety concerns. The latest disclosure “adds to the safety overhang” surrounding cellular medicines that, like zola-cel, are rapidly manufactured, wrote William Blair analyst Matt Phipps. 

The Treasury Department proposed new rules that could complicate U.S. investment in China’s fast-rising biotechnology sector. The draft regulations unveiled Thursday would add biotech to a list of technologies subject to greater federal scrutiny under the “COINS Act.” U.S. investors, for instance, would have to tell the government about certain transactions and would be barred from pursuing others. Yet cross-border drug licensing deals involving China-originated drugs — which have skyrocketed over the last few years — may not be meaningfully affected, according to multiple reports. The Treasury is seeking public comments before finalizing the rules. 

Gilead Sciences on Thursday agreed to pay nearly $1.3 billion in cash to acquire an experimental immune disease drug from Shanghai, China-based PepStar Therapeutics. The deal hands Gilead rights to an oral medicine aimed at “IL-23R,” the target of popular treatments like Skyrizi, Tremfya and the recently approved Icotyde. Like Icotyde, PepStar’s treatment HCXT-2001 is a macrocyclic peptide, a kind of intermediate-sized drug with the strengths of small molecules as well as antibodies. HCXT-2001 has an extended half-life, though, which could give it a “differentiated approach,” the company said. The therapy is currently in Phase 1 testing.

Roche has licensed from Zymeworks full rights to a dual-acting antibody drug for lung cancer. The deal announced Friday is centered on a treatment called ZW209, a T cell engager directed at the cancer protein DLL3. Zymeworks and Roche will collaborate on a Phase 1a study, with the Swiss pharmaceutical giant taking over global development afterward. Roche is paying Zymeworks $55 million up front, another $40 million upon the start of a Phase 1b trial and could add a further $718 million should the treatment hit certain development and sales targets.

data.title: Moderna, Merck shares fall on eagerly anticipated cancer vaccine results
data.description:
A cancer vaccine developed by Moderna and Merck & Co. has lived up to its billing, meeting lofty expectations from industry watchers and physicians in slowing the return of advanced melanoma, according to data published ahead of a major medical meeting.

Moderna and Merck reported in August that a combination of the vaccine, “intismeran autogene,” and Merck’s immunotherapy Keytruda, bested Keytruda alone in a late-stage trial. That study evaluated both regimens in the “adjuvant” setting after surgical removal of a tumor. 

The companies didn’t disclose details from the trial at the time, only noting that the combination had met its main goal at an early, pre-planned data check. Nonetheless, the results were hailed by analysts as a “landmark moment” and evidence that intismeran is destined for billions of dollars in sales. Moderna’s stock price swelled more than four-fold afterwards. 

The announcement made a coming Saturday presentation from the trial at the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting this year one of the biotechnology sector’s most eagerly anticipated. Ahead of it, Wall Street investors expected the intismeran regimen to be associated with anywhere from 40% to 50% relative reduction in the risk of disease recurrence or death. 

Moderna had already stated a 35% lowering would constitute a clinically significant outcome, which itself was a high bar considering Keytruda alone hit the 43% mark when compared to a placebo.

Screenshots of the findings were leaked on social media Thursday, prompting ESMO to immediately release the closely guarded study details before the meeting. According to those findings, intismeran met its mark, as the combination cut the relative risk of disease recurrence or death by 42% compared to Keytruda alone after a median of 24.6 months.

The results fall a touch short of the 44% figure initially observed in a smaller and similarly closely watched Phase 2 trial. Long-term results from that study were even more profound, showing that the risk of relapse was nearly cut in half after five years of follow-up.

Shares of both companies immediately fell on the news, with Moderna’s stock price tumbling by nearly 25% and Merck’s by around 1%. 

Some analysts immediately rallied to both companies’ defense. A “sell-the-news reaction is playing out,” wrote William Blair analyst Myles Minter. The findings "represent a highly compelling efficacy profile and substantially clear the [physician]-defined bar for a practice-changing dataset in adjuvant melanoma,” added TD Cowen analyst Tyler Van Buren. 

RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh, however, noted that the results were on the “low end” of expectations and showed a "deterioration" from what was seen in earlier testing. 

“While approval seems likely, commercial success is far less certain,” Huynh wrote.

Investigators interviewed by BioPharma Dive argued that the data represent a possible step forward in care for a persistent type of cancer.

Even with the availability of Keytruda — one of the most successful cancer drugs in history — one-third or more of people diagnosed with late-stage melanoma will die or see their disease return within five years of treatment. Drugmakers have struggled mightily to improve upon those numbers, with “PD-1” inhibitors like Keytruda as well as other medications.

“We have tried really hard. I have led clinical trials. None of them has improved over PD-1,” said Hussein Tawbi, a professor of medicine at the MD Anderson Cancer Center and an investigator in Moderna and Merck’s study. “We were resigned to the fact that this was the best we can do for patients. And now we see we can do better.”

Adding intismeran to Keytruda also reduced the relative risk of cancer spreading to “distant” organs or tissues by 38% versus Keytruda alone, researchers found. 

The trial enrollees who got intismeran reported similar rates of side effects, although those recipients had a substantially higher frequency of fever and injection-site pain. About 7% of the people who got intismeran discontinued treatment because of an adverse event, compared with 5% of those in the comparator group.

The risk of these side effects is likely “something a lot of patients would be willing to take on” given their chance to live longer, said Janice Mehnert, director of melanoma and cutaneous medical oncology at NYU Langone Health. Mehnert was also involved in the study.  

The results are the product of decades of research into vaccines that can train the body’s immune system to better recognize and hunt down cancer cells. Several earlier projects failed because they didn’t trigger a strong enough immune response, stimulated the wrong immune cells or couldn’t overcome tumors’ ability to thwart the body’s defenses. But more recently, developers like Moderna have turned to mRNA technology popularized by COVID-19 vaccines to come up with a newer approach. 

This strategy is known as “individualized neoantigen therapy.” It involves sequencing a patient’s tumor to find cancer-specific protein flags, or “neoantigens,” and then delivering into cells mRNA that encodes for them. Their presence sparks a response from immune defenders called T cells to hunt down and destroy any cells with those proteins. 

Intismeran teaches the body to spot up to 34 neoantigens. Another developer, BioNTech, has an individualized therapy in testing in colorectal and pancreatic cancer.  

Moderna and Merck have now shown the approach can work in melanoma. But physicians and investors aren’t yet sure how broadly impactful it might be in other types of cancer or in earlier stage disease. BioNTech recently reported that its personalized vaccine failed a mid-stage trial in colorectal cancer. 

Merck and Moderna are running additional studies in lung, bladder and kidney cancer. Interim results from a mid-stage trial in kidney tumors could come later this year or in the first half of 2027, RBC analyst Huynh recently wrote in a note to investors.
